overview: Goguryeo was the largest and most martial of Korea's Three Kingdoms, holding the north of the peninsula and much of Manchuria from its mountain fortresses. Its painted tombs are the fullest picture of life in early Korea, and its art reached Japan through Baekje and its own monks.

items.text: Tomb murals show hunts, processions, wrestlers, dancers, the sun crow and the moon toad, and the four directional animals, painted with a sense of movement.
Gilt-bronze crown ornaments, earrings and belt fittings show skilled metalwork.
Buddhist sculpture and temple building grew after the religion arrived in 372; the gilt-bronze Buddha of 539 from Yeonga is the oldest dated Korean Buddhist image.
Mountain fortresses of fitted stone, built to the ridgelines, guarded the valleys and river crossings.
Iron lamellar armor for horse and rider equipped heavy cavalry, as the tomb paintings show.
The monk Sundo arrived from Former Qin with images and sutras, and the court adopted Buddhism; a Confucian academy, the Taehak, was founded the same year.
Native shamanic and ancestral rites continued alongside Buddhism and Confucian learning.
The Complex of Koguryo Tombs in North Korea and the capitals and tombs of the kingdom in China were both listed by UNESCO.
The name Korea comes from Goryeo, the tenth-century dynasty that took its name from Goguryeo.

fall.text: After decades of war with Silla and Tang China, Goguryeo fell when Pyongyang was taken in 668. Tang set up a protectorate over the north; Silla held the peninsula south of the Taedong river and pushed the Tang armies out by 676.
